rationale: A wins because it knows where the real load-bearing story is: "A 22% drop in no-shows is the number the fitness industry has been guessing at for years" builds around the only hard metric and immediately demands baseline, sample size, duration, and definition. B has usable bones, but "Mindbody's AI treats 50,000 studios' booking calendars as one data set" invents a data architecture the update never gave it, and the incumbent-vs-startup angle invents a whole competitive debate. A still flirts with overreach on ClassPass, but at least it calls the missing proof an insinuation instead of dressing it up for a reporter.
gaps_in_A: "studios get it whether or not they asked for it" overreads bundled pricing as forced rollout or adoption; the update says bundled into tiers, not automatic activation across the base.

"The company that owns ClassPass now decides which classes fill first" is a strong question but an overassertive headline; the facts do not say the assistant prioritizes ClassPass versus direct members.
"a bundled-into-existing-tiers AI feature is a margin and retention play" is plausible PE logic, not a fact in the update; A correctly marks it thin, but it is still mostly inference.
gaps_in_B: "Mindbody's AI treats 50,000 studios' booking calendars as one data set" is invented. The update says Mindbody powers bookings for 50,000+ locations and uses booking data, not that it pools all customer calendars into one model.

"the prevailing assumption is that AI-native challengers out-innovate slow incumbents" fabricates a market premise and competitor set; even B admits it needs "at least one named standalone AI-scheduling competitor."
"it's adding AI to both" is wrong on the supplied facts. The update says the new assistant is for studio scheduling; it does not say ClassPass is getting AI.
"mostly non-tech-savvy industry" is lazy color, not evidence. It adds attitude where the update supplied none.
